opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been calling "catastrophic overtraining," and it was honestly a bit of a surprise when we first saw it. The conventional wisdom has been that more pre-training data is basically always better: you get a stronger base model, and that should translate into better downstream performance after fine-tuning. What we found is that this isn't monotonic. If you take a model of a fixed size and keep pre-training it on more and more tokens, at some point the fine-tuned performance actually starts to go down, even though the pre-trained model itself keeps looking better on standard metrics.

The way I think about why this happens is in terms of sensitivity. As you pre-train longer, the parameters become progressively more sensitive to perturbations. Fine-tuning is, at the end of the day, a perturbation of those parameters. Early on, that perturbation is relatively benign: you adapt to the new task and you don't lose much of what you learned. But as the model gets overtrained, the same amount of modification causes much more forgetting of the pre-training capabilities. So you have two competing forces. More pre-training gives you a better starting point, but it also makes that starting point more fragile. The inflection point is where the increased fragility starts to outweigh the gains in base quality.

We saw this empirically. For example, with some of the smaller open models, a version trained on substantially more tokens ended up doing worse after instruction tuning than a version trained on fewer tokens. We also studied it in simpler, more controlled settings, even linear models, where you can see the same mechanism quite cleanly. That gave us some confidence that this isn't just a quirk of one particular training recipe.

As for where exactly that point is, it depends on a few things: model size, since smaller models hit it earlier for a given token budget; how aggressive your fine-tuning is, meaning learning rate and how far you move from the base; and how different the fine-tuning distribution is from pre-training. You can push the point out somewhat with gentler fine-tuning or regularization that keeps you close to the base model, but then you're also limiting how much you can adapt. So there's a real tradeoff.

The broader takeaway for me is that we shouldn't be designing pre-training in isolation. A lot of scaling decisions are made by looking at pre-training loss, but most models are going to be fine-tuned, whether that's instruction tuning, RLHF, or domain adaptation. If what you care about is the final adapted model, you need to account for that downstream step when deciding how much data to train on. Pushing token counts way past compute-optimal to get a smaller model that's cheap at inference might look great on paper, but it can come with this hidden cost in adaptability.

r001.rationale: It says the turning point comes when increased fragility from more pre-training outweighs gains in base quality.

r002.rationale: It says the turning point depends on how different the fine-tuning distribution is from pre-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss quantization or modeling it as added noise.

r004.rationale: It lists fine-tuning distribution and learning rate as factors, but does not state that fixing either makes the threshold predictable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been calling catastrophic overtraining, and it really came out of a puzzle. The dominant intuition in the field is that more pre-training is basically free lunch. You throw more tokens at the model, the base model gets better on every benchmark, and so of course the thing you build on top of it should get better too. And for a while that's what everyone saw.

But when we actually looked carefully at models that had been pre-trained for very long token horizons, we found that after fine-tuning, whether that's instruction tuning or some multimodal adaptation, the models trained on more data sometimes ended up worse than models trained on less. So the base model was better, and yet the downstream model was worse. That's a strange thing to see.

The way we've come to understand it is through the lens of sensitivity to parameter changes. As you keep pre-training, the model's parameters don't just get more knowledgeable, they also get more brittle in a particular sense. Any perturbation to the weights, whether it's random noise or the structured updates you get from fine-tuning gradients, causes a larger degradation of what the model learned during pre-training. We can actually measure this. If you take checkpoints along a pre-training run and add Gaussian noise of a fixed magnitude, the later checkpoints lose more of their capability than the earlier ones. The loss landscape is getting sharper, or the model is getting progressively more sensitive, however you want to phrase it.

So then fine-tuning is a competition between two forces. You have the benefit of starting from a better base model, and you have the cost of forgetting more of that base model's knowledge because you're more sensitive to the update. Early in pre-training the first term dominates, and more data helps. But the sensitivity keeps growing, and at some point the forgetting term overtakes the gains. That crossover is the inflection point you're asking about.

What's nice is you can see this in a very simple linear setting too, so it's not some mysterious deep learning artifact. You get the same non-monotonic curve analytically, which gave us confidence we were capturing the right mechanism.

The practical implication is a little uncomfortable, because it means the optimal amount of pre-training isn't a property of the base model alone. It depends on what you're going to do with it afterward. You can delay the inflection point with things like a smaller fine-tuning learning rate or regularization that pulls you back toward the pre-trained weights, but you can't eliminate it, and often that's just trading off how much you actually adapt to the downstream task. So I think we need to stop treating pre-training scale as unambiguously good and start thinking about it as something we're co-designing with the adaptation stage.

r001.rationale: It explains that continued pre-training increases sensitivity to fine-tuning updates, and that forgetting eventually overtakes the gains from a better base model.

r002.rationale: It says the optimal pre-training amount depends on what happens afterward, but does not state that the threshold depends on the fine-tuning data.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss quantization or explain its turning point through quantization modeled as added noise.

r004.rationale: It says a smaller learning rate can delay the inflection point, but does not state that the threshold becomes predictable when the fine-tuning distribution or learning rate is fixed.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it as a mismatch between what pre-training rewards and what the downstream task needs. More pre-training data can make a model better at its pre-training objective without necessarily making it easier to adapt with the amount of fine-tuning data you have.

For example, there might be a feature that’s very predictive during pre-training but isn’t reliable for the downstream task. As pre-training strengthens the model’s reliance on that feature, a small fine-tuning dataset may not be enough to change that behavior.

So I wouldn’t expect a universal threshold where additional data becomes harmful. The way to identify it is to hold the fine-tuning setup fixed and look at downstream performance as you scale pre-training. If pre-training performance keeps improving while performance after fine-tuning starts declining, that’s the divergence you want to understand. And then the question is: does more fine-tuning data or a different adaptation procedure resolve it, or is there a deeper mismatch between the two tasks?

r001.rationale: The response describes a mismatch and says a small fine-tuning set may not undo reliance on an unreliable feature, but it does not explain the turning point as increased brittleness outweighing further learning benefits.

r002.rationale: It mentions the available fine-tuning data and says there is no universal threshold, but does not clearly state that the pre-training amount where performance worsens depends on that fine-tuning data.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss quantization or characterize it as added noise.

r004.rationale: It recommends holding the fine-tuning setup fixed to observe downstream performance while scaling pre-training, but does not say the worsening threshold becomes predictable when the fine-tuning distribution or learning rate is fixed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that more pre-training data can improve the pre-training objective without necessarily making the model easier to fine-tune. Those are different things. So the point where it starts hurting is really defined relative to a downstream task and a particular fine-tuning procedure; it isn’t necessarily a universal threshold in the amount of data.

One way to think about it is that pre-training learns a representation, and fine-tuning has to adapt that representation using a much smaller amount of data. As you continue pre-training, you can change both what information the representation contains and how easy that information is to use or modify. So a model can become better at its original task while becoming harder to adapt with the fine-tuning setup you have.

To understand that transition, I’d want to distinguish whether the model has actually lost useful information or whether our fine-tuning procedure is simply no longer able to extract it. For example, does changing the learning rate or the amount of downstream data remove the degradation? That distinction matters before we conclude that the additional pre-training data itself is harmful.

r001.rationale: It says continued pre-training can make a model harder to adapt, but does not explain the turning point as brittleness outweighing further-learning benefits.

r002.rationale: It ties the turning point to a downstream task and fine-tuning procedure, but does not clearly state that the threshold depends on the fine-tuning data.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention quantization or added noise.

r004.rationale: It suggests checking learning rate and downstream data, but does not state that fixing the fine-tuning distribution or learning rate makes the threshold predictable.
